options.content:
#### How to read this dashboard
**The harm scale.** **Red, harm** (orange while it is one or two nodes, red from three): a node operation failed or the
node froze: runtime calls refused (in 3 or more different minutes, or on 3 or more nodes within the same 5 minutes), node software restarted, the
kubelet lost track of its pods or went silent, the heartbeat stopped for over 60 s, the node stalled on memory, the CPU
split broken. **Yellow, at risk:** the node is struggling but nothing failed: an isolated runtime error, a heartbeat
30-60 s late, its software starved of CPU or stalled on memory, disk stalls, stuck tasks, missing telemetry.
**Blue-grey, expected:** seen and normal on its own: errors in a node's first 5 minutes, pods killed for memory on a
floored node. Nodes being removed (a removal taint or a deletion begun, for their first 15 minutes, or gone within 90 s) are left out of the heartbeat, silence and
waiting checks. **Grey 'no data':** the source sent nothing; unknown, never healthy.

**When something is red:** pick the node from the table, then line its failure up with section 2 and the tab the
*Where to look next* panel names. Do not page on busy CPUs. The strongest proof of a runtime missing its deadlines is in
the node's journal: the guide's Logs Insights query (chapter 11).

**How the numbers are counted.** Counters are counted step by step from their samples, so a jump after a scrape gap
still counts, a counter that appears in the range counts from zero, and a counter whose labels change counts once.
Readings are 2 minutes (4 scrapes); memory and disk stalls are held 4 minutes, CPU waiting 6, from a node's first full
window; brief memory or disk stalls show as 'seen'. Pod start counts nodes up 15 minutes. Lines from the guide:
2% CPU waiting and 5% full stall, 60 s pod-state age, 30 s heartbeat, 90 s Service map; every other line
is this dashboard's, set from the lab's runs. Source: *A private lane for the node*, chapters 8, 9 and 11.

---
Prepared by Shane Corbett · Kubernetes Specialist (shancor@amazon.com). Please retain author attribution when sharing or adapting this dashboard.

*Prepared by **Shane Corbett · Kubernetes Specialist** · shancor@amazon.com*

**Is any node being harmed?** Read the three rows of tiles: **red is harm** (a node operation failed or the node
froze; orange while it is one or two nodes), **yellow is risk** (the node is struggling, nothing has failed yet), **blue-grey is expected** (seen, and normal
on its own). The timeline shows when each started; the table names the nodes. Pick a node to focus every panel on it.
Busy CPUs are allowed: what matters is whether the node's own software still got its turn.

A node can join and say Ready even when part of its setup failed. These panels check what metrics can prove from
outside; the per-minute check on each node writes the rest to its journal. A node that fails one is replaced, not diagnosed.

Each protected node keeps **4 vCPUs** for its own software; the pods run on the rest. The scheduler is told they are
reserved, the kubelet's static CPU manager keeps pods off them, and a containerd plugin moves the listed agents onto them.

A process can own its CPUs and still sleep in the kernel waiting for the disk. **Full I/O stall** is time when every
task on the node waited on it. The runtime's own deadline errors at teardown are in the node's journal, not in metrics:
the guide's chapter 11 gives a Logs Insights query for them.

**For engineers, not for triage.** These charts show how the machinery behaves and have no harm line of their own;
read them only after section 1 has named a node and a time.

Reserved CPUs do not reserve memory. When the pods fill theirs, the kernel takes pages from everyone, including the
**kubelet's and containerd's own code**; they read it back from disk again and again and the node can freeze. A floor
(`memory.min`, set at boot from maxPods) keeps their pages in memory, so the node kills a pod instead of freezing.

Three things can go wrong: the node's **Service map** (kube-proxy) is out of date, packets are **dropped before an
application reads them** (a receive backlog or the instance's allowance), or there is **no free address** for a new pod.
None of these is fixed by CPU settings.

The operations the protection exists to keep working: the kubelet's calls to the container runtime, its checks of its
pods, its heartbeat, and starting and stopping pods. **These are the signals to alert on**; sections 2 and 3 only explain them.

**Not harm on its own.** These say *who was delayed* when an operation in section 1 slowed or failed. CPU waiting is
the share of time a group had work ready but no CPU: a CPU can be 100% busy and still serve every task on time. Amber is
the node's own software, violet its agents, blue the pods.

properties.value: Select a node to focus the dashboard on it.
How many harm checks crossed their line on this node: the red columns.
How many risk checks crossed their line on this node: the yellow columns.
A brief memory or disk stall: seen, not harm. Listed below harm and risk.

Failed runtime calls after the node's first 5 minutes, on a node with errors in 3 or more different minutes or within the same 5 minutes as 2 or more other nodes (errors that persist or affect several nodes, as the guide pages on).
Restarts of the kubelet or containerd after the node's first 5 minutes: a crash or an out-of-memory kill.
The kubelet's pod-state check (PLEG) went over 3 minutes without finishing: the kubelet then reports the node not Ready.
Longest heartbeat gap, when over 60 s (the reading can fall up to 30 s short of the real gap).
Minutes the kubelet's endpoint answered no scrape, after its first 2 silent minutes.
Highest share of time, held 4 minutes, every task on the node waited on memory, when over 5% (the guide: full memory stall is the harm).
Failed runtime calls after the node's first 5 minutes, in fewer than 3 different minutes and not within the same 5 minutes as 2 or more other nodes.
The kubelet's pod-state check went 1-3 minutes without finishing (the guide's line is 60 s).
Longest heartbeat gap, when 30-60 s (the guide's line is 30 s).
Mean pod start on the node once up 15 minutes, when over 4 s (image pulls included).
Highest share of time, held 6 minutes, the kubelet had work but no CPU, when over 2%.
Highest share of time, held 6 minutes, containerd had work but no CPU, when over 2%.
Highest share of time, held 4 minutes, every task of the kubelet or containerd waited on memory, when over 5%.
Highest share of time, held 4 minutes, every task on the node waited on disk, when over 5%.
The kernel's hung-task detections; one long-stuck task counts several times.
Mean time to create a pod's sandbox from the node's sixth minute, from 5 s. Slow here alone points to the CNI.
Every out-of-memory kill; a pod's kill on a floored node is expected under memory pressure.
Highest 2-minute share of time tasks stalled on memory or disk, when over 5% but not held 4 minutes: seen, not harm.

spec.description:
The node agents on the reserved CPUs (aws-node, kube-proxy, the DNS cache, the log shipper, the exporters) ranked by how long they waited for CPU: the delayed, not the busy.

**Healthy:** under 2%.

**If not:** An agent waiting several percent is off the reserved CPUs (restart containerd on that node) or the reserved CPUs are full (CPU lane tab).
